summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers the pub as an institution in the UK, including the long decline in pub numbers and its proposed causes, the origins of beer engines and pub names, and the role of signs in an illiterate medieval population. It also covers regulatory history: Richard II's 1393 sign law, Scotland's and Northern Ireland's flexible licensing, and the Licensing Act 2003, which allowed longer opening hours in England and Wales. It closes with notable London pubs such as the Red Lion, the Punch Bowl and the Coleherne.
one_line: Overview of the British pub: its decline, beer engines, origins of pub names and signs, licensing law changes, and notable London pubs.
key_facts: The number of pubs in the UK has declined year on year, at least since 1982.
Proposed causes of the pub decline include the smoking ban of 2007, competition from gastro-pubs, cheap alcohol in supermarkets and the general economic climate.
A beer engine is a device for pumping beer, originally manually operated, typically used to dispense beer from a cask or container in a pub's basement or cellar.
The London Gazette of 17 March 1691 published a patent in favour of John Lofting for a fire engine, and recommended another of his inventions, a beer pump.
The Bag o'Nails is said to be a corruption of Bacchanals, and The Goat and Compasses a corruption of God Encompasseth Us.
In 1393 King Richard II compelled landlords to erect signs outside their premises, so that alehouses were easily visible to borough ale tasters.
William Shakespeare's father, John Shakespeare, was one such borough ale taster.
Scotland's and Northern Ireland's licensing laws have long been more flexible, allowing local authorities to set pub opening and closing times.
In Scotland, wartime licensing laws stayed in force until 1976, following a late repeal.
The Licensing Act 2003 came into force on 24 November 2005 and consolidated many laws into a single Act.
Under the Licensing Act 2003, pubs in England and Wales could apply to the local council for the opening hours of their choice.
Alcohol was involved in 207,800 hospital admissions in 2006/7, and alcohol-related hospital admissions rose following the change in the law.
By the time the Licensing Act 2003 took effect, 60,326 establishments had applied for longer hours and 1,121 had applied for a 24-hour licence to sell alcohol.
The Red Lion in Parliament Square is close to the Palace of Westminster and has a Division bell that summons MPs back to the chamber for votes.
The Punch Bowl in Mayfair was at one time jointly owned by Madonna and Guy Ritchie.
The Coleherne public house in Earls Court was a well-known gay pub from the 1950s, and serial killer Colin Ireland used it to pick up victims.
